title: If approved Arkis policy changes are not executed, Spark must withdraw all funding from the platform
content:
A.6.1.1.1.3.7.1.2 splits execution of approved policy changes by where the component lives: "Spark Governance (for onchain updates under Spark governance admin control), or **via the Arkis team** (for offchain components including the Arkis Margin engine or CEX subaccount management)." Changes "must be executed promptly after Root Edit Primitive approval." Then the consequence: "**If policy changes are not executed as required, Spark must remove all funding allocated through the Arkis protocol infrastructure as soon as reasonably practicable.**"

The structural problem is real and general. Half of Spark's risk controls here — the margin engine, the exchange subaccounts — run on infrastructure Spark does not operate and cannot unilaterally reconfigure. A governance vote can amend the Spark Artifact; it cannot make a third party's engineers deploy a change.

Most agreements answer this with a contractual obligation and a legal remedy, which is slow, expensive, and useless when the exposure is live capital under someone else's margin logic. Spark instead pre-commits to the only remedy it can actually execute alone: leaving. The obligation is on Spark — "Spark **must** remove all funding" — not on Arkis to comply.

Making it mandatory rather than permitted is what gives it force. A right to withdraw invites case-by-case argument about whether this particular delay warrants disruption, and the answer is almost always no until it is catastrophically yes. A duty to withdraw removes the negotiation and hands Arkis a standing commercial incentive to execute promptly, since the counterparty's exit is automatic rather than discretionary.

It is the same philosophy as the Aave revenue-share pause and the term-end delegate lapse: make the safe outcome the default and let inaction produce it.
description: Off-chain components depend on the Arkis team to implement, so the remedy for non-execution is a mandated exit rather than a contractual claim Spark cannot practically enforce.
